title: Character Expression Sheets From Real AI Films
summary: 10 character expression sheets from real AI films, from photoreal to cartoon and anime, each with the exact prompt that made it. Copy the layout for your own.
body_markdown:
### What is a character expression sheet?


A character expression sheet is a reference page that shows one character's face in several emotions, such as happy, sad and angry. Animators and comic artists use it to keep a character recognisable, and AI filmmakers use it as a reference image.


### How many expressions should an expression sheet have?


Most sheets show six, which is what 7 of the 10 on this page ask for, but three can be enough. Choose the number from your story: a sheet needs the emotions the character will actually show on screen.


### What emotions should I include on an expression sheet?


Start with neutral, happy, sad, angry and surprised, then replace any that do not fit with ones from your script, such as guarded or quietly determined. A character's default resting face is often the most useful panel.


### How do you draw an expression sheet?


Draw the same head several times in a grid at one size and angle, and change the eyes, brows and mouth while the rest stays fixed. To generate one instead, describe the same grid in a prompt and attach an image of your character.


### What is the difference between an expression sheet and a character sheet?


An expression sheet shows emotions on the face, while a character sheet or turnaround shows the whole design from several angles. They can share a page, with small labeled faces under the body views.


### Is there a free character expression sheet template?


Yes. The template on this page is free to copy into any image model that takes a reference image. It is built from the wording of real prompts used for sheets in Flick films.


### Can AI make a character expression sheet from one image?


Yes, as long as the prompt says it is the same character and the model takes a reference image. Check each panel afterwards, because small details such as hair, glasses or tattoos are often the first to drift.
